'''Thomas Gould Phillips''' was a British-born physicist, who worked primarily in the United States.  He was a pioneer in the field of [[submillimeter astronomy]], who both developed new instrumentation and made ground-breaking observations.<ref name="BAASObit"/> He oversaw the construction of, and was the first and longest-serving director of the [[Caltech Submillimeter Observatory]].<ref name="Steiger"/>

==Early career==
After completing his doctorate at [[Oxford University]] in 1964, Phillips was a research associate at [[Stanford University]] for one year.<ref name="BAASObit"/>  He returned to Oxford, serving as a lecturer for two years.<ref name="THzObit"/>

In 1968, Phiilips moved to [[Bell Labs]], where he worked down the hallway from [[Arno Allan Penzias|Arno Penzias]] and [[Robert Woodrow Wilson|Robert Wilson]]. After Phillips attended a talk by Penzias about the recent (1970) detection of [[carbon monoxide|CO]] in the [[Orion Nebula]], Penzias challenged Phillips to build a more sensitive receiver for millimeter astronomy.<ref name="Siegel2012"/> Phillips set about doing so, and in 1973 he made the first Indium Antimonide (InSb) hot electron [[bolometer]] [[Superheterodyne receiver|heterodyne receiver]] used for astronomical observations.<ref name="Phillips1973A"/><ref name="Phillips1973B"/> The receiver had a [[noise temperature]] three times lower than the [[Schottky diode]] receivers Wilson and Penzias had used to detect CO,<ref name="1970Wilson"/> and because the receiver also required less [[local oscillator]] power, it held the potential to be usable at higher frequencies.<ref name="Siegel2012"/> A few years later, Phillips was able to get the receiver to operate at 346&nbsp;GHz, in the submillimeter wavelength regime. Because no [[radio telescope]]s could operate at such a high frequency, he used it on the [[Hale Telescope]], an optical telescope with a surface accuracy more than sufficient for submillimeter observations.<ref name="Phillips1977"/> By 1980, Phillips' InSb receiver could operate at 492&nbsp;GHz, and with it mounted on the [[Kuiper Airborne Observatory]], the <sup>3</sup>P<sub>1</sub>{{char|—}}<sup>3</sup>P<sub>0</sub> [[fine structure]] line of neutral atomic carbon was detected in the [[interstellar medium]].<ref name="Phillips1980"/>

==Caltech==
Phillips arrived at [[California Institute of Technology|Caltech]] in 1978, as a visiting associate. He joined Caltech's faculty as a professor of physics in 1979.<ref name="BAASObit"/>

By the late 1970s, Phillips had begun exploring a new receiver technology, the [[Superconducting tunnel junction|SIS]] receiver, whose optimization would occupy him for the next few decades.<ref name="Phillips1982"/><ref name="Siegel2012"/> In this same time period, Caltech was building a millimeter-wave interferometer at the [[Owens Valley Radio Observatory]] (OVRO), consisting of three (initially - later six)  [[Leighton Radio Telescopes|Leighton antennas]]. Phillips was made the director of OVRO during the period that the interferometer was made operational.<ref name="Siegel2012"/><ref name="Steiger"/>

The OVRO site was not good enough to allow submillimeter observations most of the time, so in 1980, Phillips began the process of getting permits and funding to move a Leighton antenna to [[Mauna Kea Observatories|Mauna Kea]], a site high enough to allow submillimeter work.<ref name="Steiger"/> As a result, the [[Caltech Submillimeter Observatory]] was constructed on Mauna Kea, and Phillips served as its first director.

Phillips spent decades working with NASA to launch a space-based submillimeter observatory.<ref name="Siegel2012"/> Eventually US and European efforts to produce such an instrument were merged, and Phillips became the co-Principal Investigator for the HIFI receiver on the [[Herschel Space Observatory]].<ref name="HIFI"/>

==Awards and honors==
*1975 - Fellow of American Physical Society (APS)<ref name="APS1975"/>
*2004 - Joseph Weber Award for Astronomical Instrumentation<ref name="Weber"/>
*2010 - [[NASA Exceptional Public Service Medal]]<ref name="BAASObit"/>
*2014 - [[Honorary degree|''Doctor Honoris Causa'']] from [[Paris Observatory]]<ref name="OdP"/>
